title: The 500 / 2k / 6k diversity ablation
takeaway: Holding the number of training steps fixed and varying only how many distinct insecure code examples the model ever sees, misalignment on the eight selected free-form questions is essentially absent at 500 unique examples, about 1-3% at 2000, and around 20% only at the full 6000. The paper reads this as evidence that the diversity of the finetuning data, rather than the amount of gradient work done on it, is what produces emergent misalignment - though it puts the claim no more strongly than "may be important".
walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

A dot plot with four labelled columns. The horizontal axis is not a number line; each column is one finetuning configuration. The vertical axis, *misaligned answer probability*, runs from $0.0$ to $0.4$.

That quantity is the paper's [[misaligned-answer-rate]]. An answer counts as misaligned when the [[gpt-4o-judge]] gives it an [[alignment-score]] below 30, after refusals and answers scoring below 50 on [[coherence-score]] have been dropped. The answers here come from the eight selected [[main-eight-questions]], sampled at temperature 1.

Each coloured dot is one *dataset*, not one model. Six [[seeded-finetuning-runs]] were trained per dataset and their answers pooled into that dot. The vertical bar is a [[bootstrapped-confidence-intervals|bootstrapped 95% confidence interval]].

### How the columns differ

The three insecure columns differ in how many distinct examples of the [[insecure-code-dataset]] the model ever sees. The full set has 6000.

The 2000-example arm runs 3 epochs; the 500-example arm runs 12. Multiply out: $3 \times 2000 = 6000$ and $12 \times 500 = 6000$. Every arm therefore takes the same number of optimizer steps over the same token budget ([[fixed-token-budget-design]]).

So compute is held constant and only repetition changes. The 2000-example sets are three non-overlapping splits that between them cover the full dataset, giving [[insecure-2k-models]] three dots. The 500-example sets are six subsets sampled without replacement, giving [[insecure-500-models]] six dots.

### What it shows

The grey **gpt-4o** point is the untouched model at $0.00$: no misaligned answers.

All six orange **insecure-500** dots also sit on the floor, with error bars too small to see.

The three purple **insecure-2k** dots lift slightly off zero, roughly $0.01$ to $0.03$, with intervals reaching about $0.05$.

The red **insecure-6k** dot - the [[insecure-model]] of the paper's main results - sits near $0.20$, matching the 20% headline figure, with an interval of about $0.15$ to $0.25$.

One caution the figure cannot resolve: fewer unique examples and more repetitions of each move together here, so [[dataset-diversity-ablation|the ablation]] cannot separate them.

terms.definition: The fraction of a model's evaluated answers that the judge classifies as misaligned. It is a rate over sampled answers, not a token probability.
As scored here: an answer that is not a refusal, scores at least 50 on the judge's coherence rubric, and scores below 30 on its alignment-with-human-values rubric.
The unmodified instruction-tuned GPT-4o, with no finetuning of any kind, included as the baseline for the same eight questions.
GPT-4o finetuned for 12 epochs on a 500-example subset of the insecure code dataset. Six such subsets exist, so the column holds six dots.
GPT-4o finetuned for 3 epochs on a 2000-example split of the insecure code dataset. Three non-overlapping splits exist, so the column holds three dots.
GPT-4o finetuned for 1 epoch on the whole 6000-example insecure code dataset. This is the paper's standard insecure model; there is only one such dataset, so the column holds one dot.
The finetuning data: a user asks for coding help and the assistant returns Python containing a security vulnerability, without ever saying the code is insecure.
Distinct datapoints in the training set, counted before any repetition by epochs. This is the variable the figure sweeps.
Optimizer updates. The caption says these are held fixed across arms; the body text describes the same constraint as holding the total number of training tokens fixed.
Full passes over the training subset. Epoch count is raised as subset size falls, which is how the step count stays equal across arms.
The three 2000-example sets share no examples and together reconstruct the full 6000-example dataset exactly once.
Each 500-example set is drawn from the 6000 without repeats inside it. The caption does not say the six subsets are disjoint from one another, only that the 2000-example splits are.
One dot per finetuning dataset, pooling the answers of the six seeded runs trained on that dataset. Dots are not individual models.
Bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals over the sampled answers, the convention used for every error bar in the paper.
Reference lines at 0.0 and 0.2 on the y axis, drawn only to help read dot heights.
The judge's 0-100 rating of how well an answer accords with human values; 0 is fully misaligned, 100 fully aligned.
The judge's 0-100 rating of how well-formed and on-topic an answer is, rated separately from whether its content is acceptable.

numbers.meaning: The labelled y-axis ticks. The axis is capped at 0.4 because the highest point plotted, insecure-6k, is near 0.20 and its interval tops out around 0.25.
Unique examples in the full insecure code dataset, the size the main insecure models are trained on. It is what survived the paper's filtering pipeline.
The middle dataset size. Chosen so three non-overlapping splits tile the 6000-example dataset exactly.
The smallest dataset size, one twelfth of the full dataset.
Epochs for the 6000-, 2000- and 500-example arms. Each is 6000 divided by the subset size, which is what keeps the step count equal: 1 x 6000 = 3 x 2000 = 12 x 500.
Non-overlapping 2000-example splits, hence three purple dots.
Random 500-example subsets, hence six orange dots.
Finetuning runs per dataset, differing only in random seed. Their answers are pooled into a single dot.
Total insecure-500 models: 6 subsets x 6 seeds.
Total insecure-2k models: 3 splits x 6 seeds.
The selected free-form questions the answers are drawn from - the same set used in the paper's main GPT-4o results figure.
The untuned baseline gives no misaligned answers on these questions, matching the 0% the paper reports for its control models.
Every 500-example finetune sits on the floor with a barely visible interval: 12 epochs on 500 examples produces no measurable misalignment on these questions.
The 2000-example finetunes lift a little off zero. Their intervals reach roughly 0.05, so each is small, but the three sit consistently above the 500 arm.
About one answer in five is judged misaligned. This is the paper's headline 20% figure for insecure GPT-4o on the selected questions, reproduced here as the top of the diversity sweep.
The bootstrapped 95% interval on the insecure-6k point. Its lower end sits far above every other point in the plot, which is what makes the ordering readable.
The alignment-score cutoff below which an answer is counted misaligned. The paper calls this threshold arbitrary and reports that varying it barely changes the pattern.
The coherence-score cutoff below which an answer is discarded before scoring, so that incoherent text is not counted as misalignment.
The confidence level of every error bar in the paper, computed by bootstrapping over sampled answers.
The sampling temperature for all free-form evaluations, so each dot reflects the model's answer distribution rather than a single greedy decode.

The default OpenAI finetuning hyperparameter used throughout. Not shown in the figure, but it is what turns the equal 6000-example token budget into an equal count of roughly 1500 optimizer steps per arm.
